deep.reconstruction:
This folio contains no mathematical derivations, computations or formulas. It is a sequence of programmatic aphorisms about mathematics, physics and foundations, separated by horizontal rules. In order:

(1) For 100 years mathematics has only increased its 'inner energy'. It must now radiate outward, or it will consume itself. This is a thermodynamic metaphor for applying mathematics to other sciences.

(2) Hilbert rejects the objection that physics is not yet far enough along to be axiomatized. Every science, at every time, is not only ripe for axiomatization but necessarily requires it, 'rightly understood'. This is the programme of the 6th Paris problem (1900).

(3) Mathematicians should see the physicists' ansätze as the correct beginning of a rigorous theory. What the physicist calls 'neglect' (Vernachlässigung) is really a rigorous limit passage (Grenzübergang). A genuine neglect would give a wrong result, whereas the physicist wants correct formulas that agree with experience. In modern terms, an approximation such as dropping higher-order terms is read as the leading term of an asymptotic limit (eps -> 0). This methodological stance shows up in Hilbert's kinetic gas theory (1912) and in the continuum-limit programme of the 6th problem. Nothing is computed.

(4) Annoyance at one's own stupidity is the spur to doing mathematics. The physicist can always plead material difficulty or lack of money for experiments.

(5) Autobiographical note on foundations. As a Privatdozent (Königsberg, 1886-92) Hilbert wanted to go back only as far as the integers. He presupposed integer arithmetic and declared the study of it to be philosophy. 'That took its revenge when I found the concept of the set of all sets.' Now one must go back to the axioms, to logic itself. The higher one builds, the broader the foundation must be. This is Hilbert's own testimony to his discovery of the antinomy of the set of all sets (the 'Hilbert paradox', known to Zermelo).

(6) Unfinished sentence: 'Mathematics, rightly developed (as one must strive for), is called upon to take over the role ...'. An insertion mark (a crossed 'A') sits at the foot of the page. The continuation is the opening line of the page supplied as 'previous': '... die früher die Philosophie spielte. Nur als Mathematiker bin ich in der Lage zugleich mit Husserl und Nernst ... zu verkehren.' So the full thought is that mathematics should take over the role formerly played by philosophy. The cross-reference suggests the 'previous' page was written after this one, or that the folio order does not follow writing order.
errors: No mathematical steps on the page, so nothing to check for mathematical errors.

The claim that a physicist's 'neglect' is always a strict limit passage is programmatic. It is not generally true as stated: many physical approximations are uncontrolled or asymptotic but not convergent. Hilbert offers no justification here.

results.what: Hilbert's report that he 'found the concept of the set of all sets' and that this forced foundations back to axioms and logic (Hilbert's paradox)
results.modern_name: Antinomy of the set of all sets / Hilbert's paradox (cf. Cantor's paradox, Russell-Zermelo paradox)
results.usually_credited_to: Cantor (1897-99, letters) and Russell/Zermelo (1901-03); Hilbert's own version reconstructed by Peckhaus & Kahle (2002) from the Hilbert Nachlass

results.what: Every science, at every time, is ripe for and requires axiomatization; physics included
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert (1900, 1918 'Axiomatisches Denken'); studied by L. Corry

results.what: Physicists' 'neglect' reinterpreted as a rigorous limit passage
results.modern_name: Rigorous derivation of approximations as asymptotic or scaling limits (e.g. hydrodynamic limit of kinetic theory)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is aphoristic and has no mathematics. The one substantive historical item is Hilbert's first-person claim to have found the 'set of all sets' antinomy. That is already documented in the literature from these same Cod. Ms. Hilbert 600 notebooks (Peckhaus & Kahle 2002), and his views on the axiomatization of physics are well studied (Corry 2004). The page is a valuable primary source but contains nothing new.
